newsitem.title: UK: Treasuries steady in London, short-end offers value.
newsitem.headline: Treasuries steady in London, short-end offers value.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries were steady to firmer in London on Monday after overnight buying from Japanese investors looking for a yield pick-up and cashing in on dollar strength.
And with little to distract the market until Friday's producer price and retail sales data, analysts expected a fairly subdued day's trading underpinned around current levels.
"We should be okay until Friday when we get key PPI and retail sales data -- the market will be looking to those for further direction," said Yamaichi International bond strategist Adam Chester.
The U.S. 30-year bond was at 94-02, yielding 7.11 percent by 1000 GMT, compared with 93-31 in Tokyo and 93-28 at the New York close.
Chester said with the market already pricing in a further rate rise, there would likely come a point when things look oversold.
"We think PPI will be relatively subdued on Friday. That may be combined with reasonably strong retail sales but I think that's already been priced in," said Chester.
"Overall we're relatively optimistic at these levels. There may be some potential for short covering to lead the market a little higher."
According to a Reuters survey, economists expect headline producer prices to be unchanged in March and retail sales to rise 0.6 percent, down from February's 0.8 percent rise.
One trader at a U.S. house here also saw the market edging higher during the week.
"We seem to have had some positive surprises on inflation lately so we might see prices do a little better throughout the week," he said.
"All the bad news has been so well publicised it's pretty much been discounted."
Analysts said the stronger dollar gave some underlying support to the market, but was not a major factor in Treasury strength.
"It gives a good tone to the market but it's not like Italy for example, where the currency and bond market hold hands all the time," said the trader.
By mid-morning the dollar had hit a fresh four-year high against the yen in Europe. By 1000 GMT the dollar/yen rate was at 125.30/45.
The trader said he'd seen some swap interest in the three to five year sector.

Yamaichi's Chester said with two year yields at 6.4 percent -- 90 basis points above the fed funds rate -- the short end of the curve offered most value. Analysts said February consumer credit data due 1900 GMT was unlikely to excite the market.
According to a Reuters survey, economists expect consumer credit to rise by $6.7 billion in February, down from a previous $8.4 billion.
